📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner. It’s your house, your rules. Our only suggestion: Make it festive, fun, and at least a little decadent.

A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November. If a major bloomin’ bird just isn’t ca-caw-caw-calling your name this year, serve a whole roast fish, pork tenderloin with sour-sweet cherry sauce, or a flaky carrot Wellington instead.

It has been revealed that or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a substantial pot of chili. You can do that. Below, find vegetarian centerpieces, celebratory roasts, chicken dinners, and seafood mains for a Thanksgiving that looks a little different. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie can stay.

Can carrots really count as a main course? They can when they’re roasted, glazed, and tucked into puff pastry with goat cheese, Gruyère, and walnuts. This Wellington feeds 8 to 10.

Red wine, browned mushrooms, pearl onions, and carrots give this meatless braise plenty of heft. Ladle it over mashed potatoes for a vegetarian anchor to your Thanksgiving menu.

Ruffled savoy cabbage, melty cheese, and a buttery cream cheese crust make this free-form tart worthy of the holiday table. Cut generous wedges for dinner and stick with savoy: Ordinary green cabbage won’t work here.

A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that turkey isn’t the only holiday cooking project worth clearing the counter for. Delicate homemade crepes are rolled around ricotta, mozzarella, and Parmesan, then baked in marinara. Make the batter and filling a day ahead to split up the work.

According to recent reports, kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

This autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

According to recent reports, british beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

It has been revealed that these impossibly tender short ribs are begging to be served with mashed potatoes and buttery milk buns with garlic butter. Give them what they want—and give yourself a head start by braising the ribs the day before Thanksgiving.

Sources indicate that brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →.

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

In a recent development, ayesha Curry’s spice-crusted prime rib takes its cues from her mother’s braised oxtails, with habanero crema on the side. Prefer a simpler garlic-and-rosemary approach? Try this Low-and-Slow Rib Roast.

Recent findings suggest that for a roast-and-sides Thanksgiving without the turkey, garlic-and-rosemary-rubbed beef tenderloin makes an excellent centerpiece. Rosemary butter dresses the sliced roast, while tangy horseradish yogurt gives everyone something to swipe their next bite through.

Toasted rice, fried onions, and garlic form a dark, peppery crust on this slow-braised pork shoulder. Set out the big platter and pass the coconut-vinegar pan sauce; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Maybe save the brown sugar-glazed ham for Christmas? This whole leg of lamb makes for a centerpiece that’s just as showstopping. And, like ham and turkey, leftover lamb can be deliciously repurposed in sandwiches.

According to recent reports, A platter of sliced pork tenderloin with glossy cherries and browned shallots has plenty of holiday presence without a long roast. Honey and red wine vinegar give the sauce its sweet-sour bite, and frozen cherries are welcome here.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re going to make tamales, it’s a good idea to make a lot of them. Better yet, turn the process into a party, with everyone spreading masa and folding corn husks around the red chile pork filling.

Industry observers note that this pasta packs a whole spectrum of holiday flavors into each bite, with crumbles of Italian sausage, shreds of brussels sprouts, and toasted pecans. Streamlining dinner into one dish leaves you more time for Thanksgiving pies.

For some people, spending all Thanksgiving in the kitchen sounds like a good time. For everyone else, there’s this beef-and-bean chili. A can of pumpkin purée thickens the broth, keeping things seasonal without calling for a single roasting pan.

Give homemade fried chicken an even more festive angle with sage and thyme in the dredge and cranberry-mustard sauce for dipping. Start the buttermilk marinade the day before.

This whole roast duck comes with a built-in Thanksgiving side: The duck fat drippings go into basmati rice that cooks while the bird rests. Strategy for an overnight dry brine before the glossy pomegranate-honey glaze gets its moment.

Industry observers note that cooking for a smaller crowd? This skillet delivers the stuffing and the bird—chicken thighs, in this case—in one tidy package. Rendered chicken fat enriches the boxed stuffing mix, with dried cranberries and lemon zest brightening things up.

Two diminutive birds make a festive roast for four. A fiery guajillo chile, ginger, and vinegar marinade flavors both the hens and the potatoes beneath them, so the platter arrives with its own very good side.

You just need to make green beans, because this Thanksgiving main is already a two-in-one: Thinly sliced potatoes cook beneath a whole chicken, catching its drippings and crisping around the edges in the same cast-iron skillet.

Sources indicate that if your Thanksgiving table could use a little red sauce (and spice), skip the whole bird in favor of this take on chicken parm. Gochujang and gochugaru bring the heat; melted mozzarella keeps things gloriously gooey.

José Andrés turns chicken wings and a colorful assortment of vegetables into a grand centerpiece, with saffron and smoked paprika flavoring the rice. You’ll need a 15" paella pan or comparably sized two-handled cast-iron or cast-aluminum pan.

It has been revealed that there’s nothing like pasta to stretch a spendy ingredient (hello, lobster). Serve with a significant crunchy salad with Italian dressing and garlic confit toast that diners can pass around for Thanksgiving party vibes.

Presenting a whole fish at the holiday table is wildly celebratory, even when you’re cooking for just two or three. Bring out lettuce wraps, kimchi, rice, and ssamjang so everyone can build each bite a little differently.

A large roasted salmon fillet looks right at home on a holiday platter, especially under a crunchy, garlicky nut salsa. Make the salsa up to four days ahead, then roast the fish when it’s time for dinner.

Sources indicate that the stuffing doesn’t have to be a side. Here, crushed boxed stuffing mix joins Parmesan, lemon zest, and parsley in a crisp crust for mustard-coated white fish. Dinner lands on the table in 25 minutes.

It has been revealed that this dark, glossy coconut caramel—savory with fish sauce and garlic, sharp with pickled jalapeño brine—turns pan-seared salmon into a holiday-worthy main. Serve with rice to catch every last bit of sauce.

Like many of the best Thanksgiving dishes, this one starts with a good stock. Carla Hall builds a fennel potlikker with celery, onions, and Pernod before layering those flavors into a hearty bowl of shrimp and grits.

Tech Report: The 8 Best Portable Air Conditioners for When You Don’t Want to Install a Window Unit

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Unlike window air conditioners, portable air conditioners roll easily from room to room and take only minutes to set up—no brackets, no tools, no sweating through a complicated installation before you can start sweating less.
  • Portable air conditioners have an internal fan that moves hot, humid air over a refrigerant-gas-filled coil to cool and expel it into a room to lower the temperature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Unlike window air conditioners, portable air conditioners roll easily from room to room and take only minutes to set up—no brackets, no tools, no sweating through a complicated installation before you can start sweating less. Most just require a nearby window and wall outlet to get cold air flowing. Yes, they tend to cost a bit more than window units, but the tradeoff is real: you can’t beat the convenience their portability adds, which is why many people choose them over other models. Plus your view isn’t blocked by a giant metal box.

Portable air conditioners have an internal fan that moves hot, humid air over a refrigerant-gas-filled coil to cool and expel it into a room to lower the temperature. The moisture it strips from the air collects in an internal reservoir that you’ll periodically need to drain. Higher-end units either pump it out automatically or evaporate it entirely so you never have to think about it. Because the whole unit rolls on casters, you can take the cold air with you instead of running more energy intensive central a/c or buying multiple window units.

It has been revealed that to find the best models to recommend, we tested air conditioners from trusted brands like LG, GE, Black + Decker, Midea, Hisense, and more. These are the units that stood out and are worth the investment.

We placed each unit in its own room and directed its discharge hose to the outside, then set the appliance’s temperature to 68 degrees and its fan speed to maximum. We directed the cold air each unit discharged at a target 8 feet away, then used an infrared thermometer to measure the temperature at four different locations on the target. We also checked the appliance’s outlet to see if it maintained a consistent temperature. To test the wheels’ durability and noise, we rolled each unit on a hard surface to maximize squeaks and rattles.

Industry observers note that we also sent several air conditioners to our staff’s homes and apartments for further testing, where our editors used them over the course of weeks within the living spaces. We tested how easy they were to use, how they operated over time, and how easy they were to integrate into daily life.

In a recent development, for our most recent enhancement, we identified the most trusted brands and surveyed current models across a range of price points, BTU capacities, and capabilities, making sure we had options for small rooms and larger ones. From there, we narrowed the field by prioritizing units with strong efficiency ratings, straightforward setup, and drainage designs that won’t require constant attention.

Our top-rated portable air conditioner stands out for how promptly it cools down a room. During testing, we turned it on and almost immediately began feeling a cold blast of air with very little runtime. The a/c noticeably brought down the temperature in just a few minutes, plus it did so quietly. According to LG, the unit operates at just 44 decibels on its lowest setting.

According to recent reports, the unit has three modes: cooling, fan, and dry. Cooling and fan are pretty straightforward while dry actually turns the unit into a dehumidifier. So, when you don’t actively need it, feel free to have it run in moist spaces like your laundry room or garage.

The louvers on the a/c unit can be set to move up and down on their own. This actually made a pretty notable difference in full-room air circulation and helped get rid of hot air that sat near the ceiling.

Setup was also quite easy, as the air conditioner was almost fully assembled right out of the box. Even connecting the hose and slider into the window was intuitive and took less than 5 minutes total. With the four wheels and very basic setup, we were rolling it from room to room in no time.

Full LG Portable Air Conditioner Review.

If you’re hesitant to spend over $500 on a portable air conditioning unit, this option from Dreo is the best bang for your buck. Considering the relatively low price, its power and added features surprised us during testing.

First and foremost, the unit blasts cold air quite swiftly. In fact, it worked nearly as well as several of the more expensive units we tested. The window exhaust has a foam seal to make sure no hot exhaust or exterior air sneaks in.

Industry observers note that the air conditioner pairs with Dreo’s app for connection and precise programming, however we ended up using (and loving) the physical remote. It has 10 buttons for changing the speed and temperature, setting the air mode, operating the sleep timer, turning on the auto-swing louver function, and more. Plus, there’s an attached magnet for convent storage on top of the unit.

On the front of the unit there are manual controls and a digital display that indicates the room temperature, mode, and fan power. So whether you’re using the remote, app, or changing settings manually, you know exactly what the status is.

Full Dreo AC515S Portable Air Conditioner Review.

This Whynter’s amperage and BTU capacity position it firmly in the heavy-duty cooling category. The same applies to its dehumidifying power, with the unit capturing up to 71 pints of moisture per day. The biggest downside is that it’s also firmly in the heavy category, weighing over 70 pounds.

The portable air conditioner has a dual-hose design (intake and exhaust) for reducing the amount of condensate that the a/c collects, since it’s supposed to be removed in the exhaust air stream.

A similar model (ARC-14SH) also operates in heat pump/heater mode. For a slightly smaller model, check out the Whynter Elite ARC-122DS below.

While most units are either quiet or powerful, the GE Profile Portable A/C offers a bit of both worlds. Because of its dual-hose design, the air conditioner takes in air at a much higher rate than one that relies on the body of the unit to do this work. With more air coming in, more cold air comes out. This was definitely true during testing.

On its average setting, the a/c noticeably cooled down a mid-sized room in less than ten minutes. Holding up my hand to the vents, I felt a cold blast of air much stronger than other options I tried out. Going even further, the Profile has a turbo mode that turns the fans up to an even higher level.

The effectiveness of the cooling has do to with more than just airflow, too. This portable a/c unit also comes with auto louvers that more evenly distribute cold air by shifting the vents up and down. I particularly like this feature for apartments like mine which are a few floors up and end up with a lot of accumulated hot air near the ceiling. The auto louvers help bring down the temperature of the entire room down as opposed to just blasting cold air in one direction.

While all these features impressed me, the unit’s best quality is that it doesn’t stand out at all. This a/c is incredibly quiet. While I barely noticed the sound at normal levels, when I set the unit to quiet mode, the noise levels drop to a whisper. According to GE, quiet mode is measured at just 42 decibels, which is lower than all other options we recommend.

This makes the Profile an ideal choice for overnight use or in small rooms. However, the remote control buttons don’t light up, so if you’re using it at night, you may need a flashlight, phone, or bedside lamp.

Full GE Profile Portable Air Conditioner Review.

If the other units on this list take up more real estate than you have or want to give, the Dreo AC319S is the one you won’t have to make room for. It's the most compact refrigerant-based portable air conditioner we've included—at just over 17 inches wide and 28 inches tall, it slips into corners and tight apartments where bulkier units don't fit. Be warned, though, the tradeoff for that smaller footprint is smaller cooling coverage. This one is best for bedrooms, home offices, and other spaces up to 300 square feet.

But what it gives up in cooling-size capabilities, it makes up for in smart features and low maintenance. The drainage-free system, powered by Dreo's patented internal pump and dual water sensors, handles condensation automatically. In moderately humid conditions, you'll likely never need to drain the unit at all. The Dreo app sends a notification if the tank does fill up, which is a thoughtful touch. That kind of hands-off convenience is why this one made our list.

Sources indicate that at just 45 decibels on its lowest setting, it's whisper-quiet on par with the priciest units here. Smart controls are also unusually comprehensive. In addition to Alexa and Google Assistant, the AC319S works with Siri, making it one of the only portable ACs that pairs nicely with Apple products. The circular LED display looks sharp, though you can’t dim it, so keep that in mind if you plan to use it overnight in rooms you want to stay dark.

According to recent reports, if you’re fortunate to have a large living room, an open-plan studio, or a finished basement, you know the luxury of size comes with a cost—cooling oversized areas can be tough. To beat the heat in big rooms, the Whynter ARC-1230WN is the unit we’d point you toward.

Sources indicate that with 14,000 BTUs, it covers up to 600 square feet—more than any other unit on this list. In independent testing, it dropped room temperature by about 12 degrees in a single hour, a result no other unit came close to matching.

According to recent reports, A big part of that performance comes from Whynter's hose-in-hose dual-hose design. Unlike a standard dual-hose setup, the intake and exhaust lines run concentrically inside a single tube, preventing heat leakage between the airstreams and improving overall efficiency. The inverter compressor, which ramps up and down rather than cycling on and off, keeps noise down once the room reaches your set temperature and reduces energy use.

In a recent development, according to Whynter, the inverter technology delivers 20 percent more cooling capacity and over 40 percent energy savings compared to non-inverter models. Do note, though, that while this is technically a portable unit, at more than 75 pounds, it’s one you’ll want to set up for the season, not haul around on the regular.

Industry observers note that if you're shopping for a portable AC because you have a room your HVAC system can’t handle, the Midea Duo MAP14HS1TBL is our top recommendation. It's a four-season unit: the same inverter-driven, hose-in-hose dual-hose design that makes it such an effective cooler works equally well in heat mode, and switching between the two is as easy as a click on the remote or SmartHome app—no setup or adjustments required.

The dual-hose design pulls in fresh air and expels exhaust air through a single concentric hose, keeping a neutral pressure balance in rooms. This prevents warm outside air from coming back in through gaps and cracks. Midea's airflow system also projects air up to 26 feet, which makes a real difference in longer rooms where less forceful units only cool the area immediately around them.

Recent findings suggest that we’re also impressed by the smart controls. The SmartHome app works on iOS, Android, and Apple Watch, and voice control is compatible with Alexa and Google Assistant. I also like that you can completely turn off the control panel lights, which is a sleep-saving feature for overnight use. And at 42 decibels on its lowest setting, it's among the quietest options we’ve come across.

We were pleasantly surprised by the power and value offered by this small portable air conditioner from Black+Decker. It begins producing cold air very rapidly, though not quite at the volume of many other air conditioners we tested. That stated, it still reduced the temperature of its target at a rapid rate.

Sources indicate that the unit provides multiple fan speeds, dedicated dehumidification, a timer setting, and a sleep setting. Note that there is no heater setting on this appliance. It’s meant to cool and dehumidify exclusively.

Reviews Editor Amber Joglar tested out the four-in-one version of this model which also functions as a heater. After just 10 minutes of use in her room, Joglar felt, “a noticeable shift in the air temperature.”.

Industry observers note that the quick cooldown times stood out across both models, though Joglar also pointed out that this led to the exhaust pipes heating up promptly as well. This isn’t necessarily a problem, but if you blueprint on using the unit for several hours a day, consider covering the tubes in insulation.

In addition to the cold air, Joglar liked the remote and LED control panel, saying, “I normally just change settings on the air conditioner itself because it’s right next to my bed, so backlit controls are helpful.”.

Similarly, the remote control is great for when she’s already in bed or wants to pre-cool the room before she’s ready to go to sleep.

Joglar’s model also heats rooms. So, instead of storing it in a closet or attic for the cold winter months, she simply switches functionality.

Read Our Full Black+Decker Portable Air Conditioner Review.

Coverage area is one of the most important factors in choosing an air conditioner. Manufacturers rate units in square footage, but that number assumes an average ceiling height (roughly eight feet) and room insulation. If the room is especially hot in the summer (for example, it’s a finished attic or it has large, south-facing windows) we recommend bumping up to the next size rather than buying a unit that will run constantly and struggle to keep up.

An air conditioner’s cooling capacity is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTU, per hour. To gauge coverage, figure roughly 20 BTU per square foot of space. Most portable a/c units range from 5,000 to 20,000 BTUs, which puts their effective range roughly between 350 and 700 square feet. So when in doubt, size up—an oversized unit cycles off when it hits your target temperature, while an undersized one never stops trying.

Single-hose units essentially recirculate the room’s air to cool it and have one line that runs outdoors to expel exhaust. The catch is that expelling air creates a slight negative pressure in the room, which pulls in warm air from other parts of the house and from outside through gaps around doors and windows. It works, but it’s working against itself.

In a recent development, dual-hose units solve this by pulling outside air in through one hose for cooling and pushing hot exhaust out through a second hose. The result is a more self-contained system that’s noticeably more efficient, especially in larger spaces. The tradeoff is price.

Sources indicate that because dual-hose models are more complex, they tend to be more expensive. If you only have a small space to cool, a portable a/c with a single hose may suit your needs just fine. For anything larger, the dual-hose design is worth seriously considering.

According to recent reports, hose length determines how far away from a window you can maneuver your portable air conditioner. If you set it up in a large room, or one where the nearest window is far from where most people gather, hose length becomes more key.

It has been revealed that it also plays a key role in room setup. If the hose isn’t long enough to set the air conditioner in front of large furniture pieces, you may have to rearrange the room for the most effective cooling. Most hoses range anywhere from 50 to 90 inches fully extended. This should give you enough space to make adjustments and pull the air conditioner closer to the center of the room if needed.

It has been revealed that most portable air conditioners hover between 50 and 60 decibels while they’re running—that’s roughly the noise level of a normal conversation. In most cases, that’s fine during the day, but if you’re planning to run the unit in a bedroom overnight, those numbers start to matter.

Units that dip below 50 decibels in their quietest modes are on par with most ceiling fans and are easier to sleep through; a few on this list get impressively close to whisper-quiet. Pay attention to the decibel rating at the unit’s lowest fan setting, not just its average operating level.

Much like larger ductless mini-split air conditioners, some portable air conditioners include a heat pump. “If you’re shopping for an a/c unit because you have a space not currently cooled or heated, one of these models may warrant consideration,” indicates gear editor Bradley Ford. “Similarly, you may have a room that your HVAC system doesn’t reach effectively. Rooms like this are typically either too cold or hot, depending on the season. If this is the case, a unit with heating capabilities may be able to fill your HVAC gap.”.

In a recent development, every portable a/c pulls moisture out of the air, similar to home dehumidifiers. The question is what happens to it next. Budget units collect it in an internal pan that you’ll need to manually drain, sometimes daily in humid conditions.

It has been revealed that other units use self-evaporating technology to push moisture out through the exhaust hose with no bucket to remember. A few high-end models go even further, offering a continuous drainage port where you can attach a hose and never think about water again. If low-maintenance matters to you, the drainage method is a factor to consider.

According to recent reports, there isn’t a clear superior option between window units and portable options. Choosing between the two largely depends on your home, windows, and personal needs. That mentioned, window air conditioning units are generally faster at bringing temperatures down and run more efficiently than their portable counterparts.

Portable air conditioners have certainly closed the gap over time in terms of cooling ability, but still lag behind if that’s your number one priority.

Industry observers note that portable units stand out because of their convenience and ease of setup. If you don’t have compatible windows, get a portable unit. If you need quick cooling in a spot that generally doesn’t need air conditioning, get a portable unit. If you want just one machine for your entire apartment, get a portable unit.

Portable air conditioners are compatible with a lot more window openings than window units, so you can use them regardless of your apartment or home fixtures.

It has been revealed that new portable a/c units are relatively energy efficient across the board. That remarked, it’s certainly a sliding scale. There are several ways in which energy efficiency is calculated for air conditioners, but the shorthand is if your a/c unit is Energy Star-certified, it’s worth getting.

For items that don’t have Energy Star certification, pay attention to the CEER, EER, and SEER numbers. In short, look for an air conditioner with a CEER above 10, with anything above 12 qualifying for Energy Star certification. Similarly, look out for a SEER above 14 in the north and 15 in the south as well as an EER above 10. These are general numbers, but serve as a basic guide when choosing between different options.

One of the biggest challenges to solve with portable air conditioners is cooling efficiency. While most units generate a ton of cold air, leakage from the hose or exhaust port can work against that. There are two key things you can do: insulate the opening in the window and insulate the hose itself.

It has been revealed that many portable units provide foam pieces that fit in and around the window insert to minimize the amount of hot air that leaks in from outside. The hose itself won’t come with foam insulation pieces, but you can perform a similar trick by buying one online or by making one yourself. Some people use blankets while others have used everything from reflective sun shades to Amazon plastic packaging. The goal is to prevent heat from the tube from radiating into your living space.

Naturally, Styles’s latest outing served up a perfectly casual-cool outfit. A sleek khaki trench coat? Check! Classic straight-leg jeans and brown leather loafers? Check-check. It’s not hard to understand why the luxurious maxi bag is such a huge hit. It fits a lot, for one, making it a utilitarian and practical choice for schlepping one’s belongings around town. (For that reason, it also makes it a great travel bag.).

Harry Styles is clearly pro-schlepping: Despite once carrying mini bags, he’s been seen wearing the very same Chanel style in a leopard-printed version, making the case for carting around ginormous bags that can carry, well, just about anything. What do you think Styles has in his spacious (but not ludicrously capacious) bag, exactly? Some prototypes of his Pleasing merch or products? An extra microphone, for when he’s ready to burst out into song? Use your imagination, Stylers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the concern could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Sources indicate that massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie revealed his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

In a recent development, speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

In a recent development, he must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

It has been revealed that if the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

According to recent reports, in an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

In a recent development, the questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

According to recent reports, massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

In a recent development, "It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie stated. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie stated: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

According to recent reports, hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries remarked. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

It has been revealed that last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

It has been revealed that referring to Massie’s measure, Smith stated, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

According to recent reports, "Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, stated in a post on X on Sunday.

Also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley stated the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Industry observers note that massie declared in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure indicates Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

According to recent reports, further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution states, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:.

According to recent reports, the House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

Do have a keen eye on your chicken (especially if you have a drawer-style broiler at the bottom of your oven), checking it every so often to prevent a completely blackened cook.

Heat broiler. Whisk ¼ cup honey, ¼ cup white miso, and 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a large bowl to combine. Add 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (the miso and soy sauce are plenty salty, so no need to season the chicken) and toss to coat. Arrange on wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet lined with foil and spoon any marinade remaining in bowl over. Broil chicken, turning halfway through, until cooked through and deeply charred in spots, 10–15 minutes (keep a close eye on it). Thinly slice chicken. Serve over steamed white rice, topped with thinly sliced scallions, if desired.

The Best Air Fryers For Faster, Crispier Cooking (2026)

📅 14 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that buzzy as they’ve become over the past several years, air fryers are really just small ovens with fans built into them, i.e., convection ovens that circulate hot air around your food.
  • Air fryers can take a few forms; the robot-esque basket-style models are probably what come to mind when you think of an air fryer, but there are versatile countertop convection ovens that add bake, broil, toast, and slow-cook options to the air fryer functionality.
  • The best for all varieties of air fryer needers are below.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that buzzy as they’ve become over the past several years, air fryers are really just small ovens with fans built into them, i.e., convection ovens that circulate hot air around your food. Our years of testing air fryers (and we’ve used over two dozen in that time) have taught us that there are plenty out there that can give you crispy-enough results—but the very best air fryers churn out not only golden brown french fries and crispy-skinned chicken wings, but tender fillets of salmon and even whole roast chickens at the touch of a button.

Air fryers can take a few forms; the robot-esque basket-style models are probably what come to mind when you think of an air fryer, but there are versatile countertop convection ovens that add bake, broil, toast, and slow-cook options to the air fryer functionality. Some even dehydrate and steam too. And most recently more bowl-style air fryers have started to hit shelves, which swap a slide-in basket for a glass container and top-down, air-frying lid.

The best for all varieties of air fryer needers are below.

Industry observers note that new in this patch: We tested five models in the growing category of glass air fryers, i.e., those with slide-in glass baskets or glass bowl bases with an air fryer lid. This included new reviews for air fryers from Cuisinart, Chefman, Kisimile, and Magnifique, plus retesting the Ninja Crispi against this new crop of similar products.

Most air fryers fit into one of three categories: oven, basket, or bowl.

A countertop convection oven, or air fryer–toaster oven, combines most of the crisping power of the basket-style air fryers you know and love with the multifunctionality you get from a toaster oven or countertop oven. Generally, the “air frying” function is achieved with a perforated slide-in rack, which usually means lots of cooking surface, but the racks are usually shallow and can require careful tossing or flipping of whatever you’re cooking, depending on the dish. But air fryer ovens, like the Breville Smart Oven Pro with its 13 different cooking modes, can do a lot, making them bona fide do-it-all kitchen appliances.

Basket-style air fryers aren’t as versatile as air fryer ovens, but they’re also less expensive and take up less space. They also tend to deliver better final results on traditional air fryer stuff like crisping up small foods that require shaking (tater tots, french fries, or brussels sprouts), for which a handled basket is far easier to maneuver. Minuses are that they can be hard to clean and limited on square inches inside the basket. They’re also sometimes made of plastic or nonstick coated materials, which may not appeal to some consumers.

It has been revealed that bowl air fryers offer some of the best (and worst) of both worlds and also some unique benefits. Most of these include a heat-resistant glass bowl acting as the basket. Some models operate much like basket air fryers, with the glass container sliding into the base unit, while others opt for a “lid” that sits on top and houses the air frying mechanism. The glass baskets make these very easy to clean (included crisping trays are another story), however their functionality for shaking and pausing to flip foods can be cumbersome. But many come with lids for the glass containers, letting them double as prep and storage containers too.

Capacity: 6 qt.Wattage: 172510 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Roast, Broil, Frozen, Preheat, Reheat, Dehydrate, Proof, Bake, and Keep WarmColor: WhiteWeight: 11.5 lb.Dimensions: 11.8" x 14.4" x 11.9"Warranty: 2 years.

It has been revealed that what we love: The 6-Quart Cosori Turboblaze Smart Air Fryer impressed us in every test, producing evenly browned and crispy frozen sweet potato fries, juicy chicken breasts, and perfectly cooked brussels sprouts. It has a straightforward digital interface that allows you to easily set the time and temperature and an impressive array of preset programs (Air Fry, Roast, Broil, Frozen, Preheat, Reheat, Dehydrate, Proof, Bake, and Keep Warm).

A few things set the Turboblaze apart from the competition (including the previous longtime winner of this test, the Instant Vortex Slim). Most notably, it consistently produced the crispiest food of any air fryer we tested in record time. That may have something to do with the fact that there’s more space between the crisper plate (where the food sits) and the bottom of the basket than there is in some of the other top-performing models we’ve tried, which allows for better air circulation.

Another standout feature is its variable fan speeds, which adjust automatically depending on the cooking function. Unlike most air fryers that use this tech behind the scenes, the Turboblaze demonstrates you the fan speed right on the display. Air Fry, for example, is one of four “turbo modes,” running the fan at full blast (speed 5), while Bake uses a gentler speed 3 to avoid disrupting delicate foods. Low-temperature settings like Dehydrate and Proof drop all the way down to speed 1.

According to recent reports, the Cosori Turboblaze is also a real value pick. The top performer in its price range (100–150) by a wide margin, it’s powerful, versatile, quiet, lightweight, and easy to clean (the brand notes both the nonstick basket and cooking tray are dishwasher-safe, though we recommend hand-washing anything with a nonstick coating).

The model we tested includes smart features, meaning you can control it remotely or use voice commands via the VeSync app. If that’s not your thing, Cosori also sells a non-smart version for about $10 less.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: Our gripes with this model are minor. It’s slightly annoying that you have to press a release button to pull the basket out. And while the greater amount of space between the crisper tray and basket bottom contributes to better airflow (and thus better browning), it means food is more likely to fall through while cooking.

Capacity: 2.1-qt.Wattage: 9004 cooking functions: Air-Fry, Bake, Roast, ReheatColors: Gray, red, white, greenWeight: 4.9 lb.Dimensions: 10.1" x 8.3" x 10.5"Warranty: 2 years.

If you’re on a tighter budget, have very little counter space to spare, or are mostly crisping up food just for yourself, consider the Cosori Lite 2.1-Quart Mini Air Fryer.

In a recent development, what we love: This compact air fryer did a beautiful job crisping and browning small servings of frozen tater tots and fries, sliced zucchini, and veggie burger patties (two at a time, max). Depending on where you buy, it will only costs $50–$60 (as of publish time)—not at all bad for a lightweight, quiet, digital air fryer with four easy-to-use presets (air-fry, roast, bake, and reheat). It’s easy to tuck into a cabinet and to clean. Like the Cosori Blaze, the Lite has a nonstick basket. Again, while the manual notes the nonstick basket is dishwasher-safe, we always recommend hand-washing anything with a nonstick coating.

What we’d leave: Per its name, it’s quite small—don’t expect to be cooking enough food for more than two people in this thing. It also won’t remind you when it’s time to shake your food, so you’ll need to keep an eye on the timer yourself (luckily, the digital display makes this pretty easy).

If you want an air fryer with maximum versatility and have some counter space to spare, spring for the Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro. Breville makes a few different models (which can be found in the kitchens of many of our editors), but this one is the best combination of performance and value.

What we love: This midrange model has been our top pick for years now because of its versatility, build quality, intuitive design, and consistently strong performance in testing.

In testing, the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro delivered reliably great results. It excelled at foods that need to be laid in a flat, even layer across the crisper tray (think veggie burgers or salmon fillets), but also handled frozen fries, tots, and sweet potato fries well. Its interior is roomy enough to fit a quarter sheet pan or 13x9" casserole pan, which means it can effectively double your oven space (or eliminate the need to turn on your full-size oven altogether).

This model is also a favorite among BA staffers and Test Kitchen editors, as well as award-winning cookbook author Nik Sharma, who developed some of BA’s favorite air fryer recipes. “I prefer toaster-oven-style to basket-style air fryers, because they’re easier to use for more common tasks like baking, toasting bread, and roasting more efficiently,” Sharma states.

Recent findings suggest that what we’d leave: As with most oven-style air fryers, it’s harder to toss or shake small foods mid-cook compared to a basket-style machine. We also found that, in general, food benefited from a higher cooking temperature (and often slightly longer cook time) relative to the basket-style winners.

Capacity: .5 cubic feetWattage: 18005 Cooking functions: Toast, Bagel, Broil, Pizza, Bake & Roast5 Air-frying functions: Air-Fry, Fries, Wings, Bacon, Crispy ReheatColor: Stainless steelWeight: 15.8 lb.Dimensions: 15.7" x 16.9" x 10"Warranty: 2 years.

If you like the idea of going the air fryer–toaster oven route but (1) don’t have the space for the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro or (2) don’t want to shell out $400 in pursuit of crispiness, here’s some good news: Breville offers the Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact, which is essentially a smaller, cheaper version of our top pick.

What we love: As with most Breville products, the Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact feels thoughtfully designed, with stainless-steel finishes and a solid build. There are fewer niche modes than the Pro—no Dehydrate or Proof—but it does include four air-frying-specific presets in addition to a standard Air Fry setting.

Industry observers note that we found using the Compact intuitive (the guide printed on the inside of the oven door helped). We also appreciated the “bit more” button, a feature borrowed from Breville’s toasters that adds a touch of extra cooking time when your fries are looking just a touch underdone.

This model performed comparably to the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro in most of our tests, producing juicy chicken, evenly browned cubes of tofu, and crispy veggies. We still prefer the larger model for its versatility and additional functionality, but this little oven would make a worthy addition to any smaller kitchen.

Sources indicate that what we’d leave: While the Compact did well in most tests, it struggled a bit with frozen sweet potato fries. This largely came down to overcrowding due to the smaller capacity: While we tried to fit an entire bag’s worth on a single tray, the unevenness with which the fries browned is a good example of the fact that, unlike a basket fryer, countertop oven-style air fryers are best used to cook things in a single layer.

As mentioned, there’s a guide to oven inserts and placement on the inside of the oven’s door, but this is easy to miss, and these suggestions did not appear in full in the manual. Because of this, one tester accidentally cooked chicken with no tray underneath the wire basket to catch the drippings, which resulted in a smoking-hot mess.

It’s also worth noting that one of the major benefits of opting for an oven-style air fryer tends to be capacity, but the Compact wasn’t able to fit more food than our top basket-style pick.

The Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact (L) is much smaller than the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro (R).

Clearview 4-Quart Glass Basket Air Fryer.

Capacity: 4 qt.Wattage: 16005 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Bake, Broil, Recrisp, Keep Warm, plus custom settingsColors: Black, Toasted Oat, Sage, TahiniWeight: 12.75 lb.Dimensions: 13.75" W x 12.75" D x 11.25" HWarranty: 3 years.

Newly introduced on the market in 2026, Cuisinart’s ClearView series of air fryers truly delivers on its name with the introduction of a glass basket model that also sports a viewing window on the top of the unit (the line also features a larger, 9-qt. non-glass model). Unlike other glass air fryers we tried, this one operates more like the basket-style most people expect when they think of an air fryer.

What we love: The ClearView got high marks across the board in our tests comparing glass air fryers head-to-head, almost always offering up the winning results. The controls are easy to navigate, and the functions are intuitive with beeps to remind you to flip or shake your food when your cook is halfway through. In addition to the usual Air Fry, Bake, and Reheat functions, Cuisinart’s also offers a Keep Warm. Plus, there are two programmable custom presets if you’re cooking the same foods frequently.

The crisper plate is nonstick, coated in PFAS-free ceramic, making it a breeze to clean with a little soap and water (or just throw it in the dishwasher). The glass basket is also dishwasher-safe. The ClearView doesn’t have any kind of mesh or grate covering the heating mechanism. We’ll continue to see how this fares over time, but in the meantime it’s nice not worrying about another greasy, perforated plate to clean. Lastly, the ClearView 4-Quart Glass Basket Air Fryer also comes in four colors—Black, Toasted Oat, Sage, and Tahini—and, as with all countertop appliances, it’s nice to have some kind of choice behind black plastic and stainless steel.

According to recent reports, what we’d leave: The cord wrap post noticeably sticks out from the back of the unit. While this is probably great for airflow safety, it adds inches to a machine that’s also tall. And unlike some of the other glass air fryers we tried, Cuisinart’s bowl is oven or microwave safe. Granted, the point of the bowl is to air-fry, but if you’re using to carry your lunch into the office after cooking the night before, reheating is a little trickier.

Capacity: 6.5 qt.Wattage: 17256 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Roast, Bake, Dehydrate, Proof, and ReheatColor: Stainless steelWeight: 14.1 lb.Dimensions: 11.8" x 11.8" x 11.6"Warranty: 5-year limited.

We won’t go down the PFAS rabbit hole and get deep into the concept of “nontoxic” cookware right here and now (we've got other articles for that), but given the way the concept has come front and center we know some people want an air fryer with a PFAS-free nonstick basket—and for that, we recommend the Cosori Iconic.

According to recent reports, what we love: It has similar features and produces similar results to our top pick, the Cosori TurboBlaze, churning out crispy-skinned salmon and beautifully browned Brussels. Like the TurboBlaze, the Iconic allows you to choose between five different fan speeds, which means it's equally adept at turning delicate kale into crispy chips without blowing them around the basket as it is cooking hefty bone-in chicken breasts to bronzed perfection.

And for those looking to eliminate PFAS from every inch of their kitchen, it has both a PFAS-free ceramic nonstick-coated basket and crisper plate.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: Aesthetically, it may not be for everyone as this stainless-steel air fryer looks a bit spaceship-like. But the real downside is the price, which is practically double that of the TurboBlaze.

Industry observers note that in the long run: The Cosori Iconic has seamlessly fit into the life of BA’s head of video, Dan Siegel. The speed is what won him over: “I shave 25% or more off any package-recommended cooking time and achieve perfect browning and crisping on every cook. The nonstick surfaces of both the basket and the included rack are remarkably easy to clean, making this my go-to appliance. My toaster oven probably misses me.” He mostly uses it for his two kids, occasionally scaling up to cook chicken breasts for his family of four, which takes two batches. (“It’s not huge.”) Despite the mirror-like stainless-steel finish, upkeep has been simple: “I haven't had any issues; I really only touch the top and the basket.” And then there’s the look. "It looks grown-up, like an actual appliance and not a massive plastic toy without looking industrial. The MacBook of air fryers.".

We have spent hours and hours over the past few years researching, testing, and retesting popular air fryers from top-name brands, including Breville, Cuisinart, Ninja, Philips, and Cosori. Here's how we put each appliance to the test:.

When evaluating each model, we looked for a few key qualities:.

4-Quart Vortex 6-in-1 Mini Air Fryer.

This model from Instant Pot is a great option if a full-size (6-qt. or more) air fryer feels too big for your space or lifestyle, but our winning mini model (2-qt. limit) is too small. There’s a lot to love here, including the intuitive controls and presets, the viewing window and built-in light, and the ceramic nonstick interior coating. In testing, we found it did a decent job crisping everything we threw at it, though its performance didn’t quite match the winning Cosori Turboblaze.

Instant Vortex Slim XL 6-Quart Air Fryer.

This model from Instant was a previous top pick, and we still think it’s an excellent air fryer. Its design, although compact, offers a significantly larger cooking surface area than comparably sized air fryers thanks to the shape of its basket. In practice, this meant our tester was able to fit an entire extra veggie burger patty (six total) compared to models of a similar size and generally cook more food in each batch without sacrificing any of the airflow that makes air-fried food so crispy.

Vortex Plus 6-Quart ClearCook Air Fryer.

In a recent development, if a basket-style air fryer is what you’re after and you like the idea of being able to monitor what you’re cooking, the Instant Pot Vortex Plus ClearCook is definitely worth considering. This model performed nearly identically to our old top pick, the Instant Vortex Slim (probably because it’s a very similar build). The major difference—besides the ClearCook’s dimensions—is that it has a cooking window located at the front of its basket, plus a button that switches on an interior light, sort of like a traditional oven. This makes tracking the progress of your tots, fries, or chicken wings possible without removing the basket and disrupting the cooking process. Considering that providing a certain level of brownness is one of the chief concerns in air fryer cooking, this really comes in handy. A few more bonus points for the ClearCook: It adds Dehydrate to its list of functions and can hold temperatures as low as 95°F (the low end of the Vortex Slim’s range is 120°F). The ClearCook also happens to be $30 cheaper than the Slim at full price. On the downside, the square shape of the ClearCook’s basket fits one less veggie burger patty than more elongated baskets. It’s also a bit bulky.

According to recent reports, the Typhur Dome 2 is notably spacious compared to other basket-style fryers, with 139.5 square inches of cooking surface that fits a 12" pizza, 20 chicken wings, or 11 large chicken thighs per batch, and a digital panel with 15 presets plus a companion app offering more settings, self-cleaning, and one-touch recipes. We used to recommend the original Typhur Dome as a top pick for extra-large capacity, but after testing the Dome 2, which replaced it, we felt its performance didn’t quite merit a spot on our top picks: When filled to capacity, it took much longer to properly cook and crisp food than most other basket air fryers, and 11 bone-in chicken thighs took upward of 45 minutes to get truly golden, a major red flag given that cutting cooking time is a major reason to choose an air fryer over the oven. That stated, the Dome 2 cooks food evenly and does eventually get very crisp, so if you’re feeding a large family and have counter space to spare, it may still be worth the investment.

It has been revealed that the Philips almost took a top spot—almost. It’s got a generous capacity, the control panel is easy to navigate, and it performs well with minimal user intervention. In other words, you won’t have to do a lot of shaking or stirring to get crispy fries from the Philips. This model did have a smaller yet heavier basket, and it’s loud and harder to clean due to a bunch of interlocking parts. It’s a good air fryer, but with its higher price tag, we feel like there are better deals on this list.

In a recent development, this newer model from Philips has a lot going for it: sleek touchscreen interface, helpful viewing window, and a whopping 16 settings. It did very well in our testing, producing crispy tots, tofu, and fries, but we preferred the design and the interface of the Cosori and Instant models. If you’re looking for an air fryer with a window feature, we’d recommend going with the Instant ClearCook (slightly cheaper at the time of writing) unless you find this model at a discount.

The Dreo ChefMaker isn't just an air fryer—it's also got probe cooking capabilities and app compatibility that make cooking proteins pretty effortless, and is a personal favorite of senior editor Olivia Tarantino. For the purposes of this article, though, we mainly tested its air frying abilities. We found that while the Dreo performed well, the winning TurboBlaze produced crispier, more evenly-cooked results all while ringing in at a third of the price. That noted, if the probe cooking feature intrigues you, this fryer might be worth a try.

Recent findings suggest that our Place partnered with James Beard Award–winning chef and cookbook author J. Kenji López-Alt on this updated version of the Wonder Oven, which features eight cooking functions, a touchscreen interface, and a roomy three-tier 30-liter capacity. Like all of Our Place's products, this little oven is an aesthete’s dream—but looks aside, it impressed us. It’s incredibly powerful, able to crisp brussels sprouts, tofu, and fries up to twice as fast as the winning Breville. It produced tender salmon with potato-chip-like skin in just seven minutes. Despite its smaller footprint, it’s large enough to fit a quarter-sheet pan, making it a good option if you want to save a few inches of counter space.

Industry observers note that all that noted, while the Wonder Oven Pro is generally well-designed, a few features were annoying to use. The touchscreen isn’t the most responsive. But the bigger matter we had was with the preheating cycle. Preheating this oven to 400°F took 8–9 minutes from cold, which is already slower than the Breville’s 4–5. But more importantly, the Breville (like most regular ovens) takes less time to preheat when it’s already at temp. The Wonder Oven Pro, on the other hand, seemed to kick off a whole latest several-minutes-long preheat cycle even when it had just been heated, only after which the timer would start.

Cuisinart Air Fryer Oven 6-Qt Basket Stainless Steel Air Fryer.

According to recent reports, the Cuisinart was easy to use, didn’t whirr too loudly, included a nice preheat feature, and was about the same price. We also really liked the viewing window you could use to check the progress of your food. However, its deeper square-shaped basket has less surface area than something like the Instant Vortex Slim’s rectangular one, which limits its capacity.

Ninja SL401 DoubleStack XL 2-Basket Air Fryer.

The DoubleStack takes the idea of a dual-basket air fryer to a whole latest level—literally. Like the Vortex Slim, the DoubleStack’s design prioritizes using vertical space. It’s skinny with the baskets stacked on top of each other instead of side by side like most other dual models. This makes it narrow and tall instead of wide, but not so tall that you can’t nestle it under your cabinets. Despite its space-saving design, you don’t lose out on actual cooking space. The baskets are big enough to fit a chicken, and the wire racks in each mean you can really maximize how much you’re cooking. (Though you do need to remain mindful of not overloading it with food, otherwise you’ll block the airflow and mess up the whole air-frying process.) You can also program the baskets separately and utilize the machine’s Smart Finish feature—which delays the start of the basket with the shorter cook—to have a whole meal ready at the same time. The one thing we didn’t like was the somewhat confusing interface.

AeroLucen 5-quart Glass Air Fryer.

Like the Cuisinart ClearView we recommend above, this glass air fryer operates like a traditional basket air fryer, in fact even more so as it features a front-mounted basket handle with slide-in operation. It’s a sleek-looking machine with a glossy top that illuminates when powered on with all of your touch-surface buttons. And we like that’s is relatively compact at just over 9.5" tall, making it great for in-cabinet storage. In the glass category, it performed nearly as well as the Cuisinart across the board with just a few cases of less even results, but we’re really nitpicking. What we didn’t like was the mesh-style crisping plate, which is tedious to clean and sits awkwardly on some jutting posts inside the basket, (though its design does offer a high and low position for maximizing space or airflow). That mesh is repeated on the underside of the heating element, something we don’t look forward to cleaning after a few dozen oil-evaporating cooking cycles. The internal light is intended to help you see what you’re cooking, but it glows red, which isn’t so helpful when you’re trying to keep an eye on browning.

Of the lid-style glass bowl air fryers we tested, this one was the easiest to maneuver with a fold-away handle that makes removing the top easy for flipping or shaking in the middle of cooking. With fine-tunable controls, it nailed crunchy skin on chicken thighs and crispy brussels sprouts with tender centers. More delicate dishes like salmon didn’t get where we wanted on the first try, and tofu cubes required more time than the recipe allotted to get anywhere near crispy enough. It fell short, as a lot of the glass bowl fryers did, on frozen fries, yielding uneven results and underdone portions when using the settings suggested on the back of the bag. We wish the “flip” alert was more than just a light, and it’s a little odd that the “Dehydrate” setting is listed as a bonus because you have to long-press another button to use it. The attached feet also mean the glass bowl can’t be put in the oven or microwave, but it is dishwasher-safe and comes with a lid. Plus, the whole fryer and basket setup is designed to nest inside itself for storage. And of this style of meal-prep-friendly air fryers, it’s the best version.

Instant Vortex Plus 4-Quart Air Fryer.

In a recent development, this Instant Pot air fryer model is if you need something with a smaller capacity. The rectangular shape of its basket made it easy to fit plenty of food inside. It is sleek and has a short profile, which are nice features too. The Vortex Slim just offered better performance.

This is Ninja's basic basket air fryer. It’s lightweight and simple to use, and it does a nice job crisping up fries. The round shape of its basket, though, makes it less versatile than other models on this list. If you’re trying to cook raw proteins or a tray of vegetables, you give away a lot of space with a round basket.

While the Dash looks cute with its retro silhouette and poppy colors, it just didn’t perform that well. Sweet potato fries came out soggy and greasy. Tofu cubes got crisped on one side but were raw on the other, and the round basket could only fit one veggie burger. The two dials, controlling time and temperature, also prevented us from getting more specific in the cook settings.

Panasonic FlashXpress Air Fryer Toaster Oven.

This oven-style air fryer from Panasonic performed well in our testing, but we found it frustrating to use for a few reasons. It has 12 different functions, but they come with very little on the display as to what each of these functions truly means. The Air Fry mode only allowed us to select temperatures between 410℉–445℉, which seemed quite high for certain foods. We also disliked the automatic preheating period that we couldn’t bypass even if the oven was already hot (this was particularly annoying when we just wanted to tack on an extra few minutes after finishing a cooking cycle). If you want to do that, you have to take the extra step of once again pressing the start button after the preheating process in order to start the timed cook cycle.

Like all of DTC darling Our Place’s products, the original Wonder Oven is cute. Unfortunately, it failed to impress us enough to earn a recommendation here. While it did fine at cooking tater tots and french fries, it produced unevenly browned, ultra mushy zucchini and tofu that never quite got the crisp exterior we were looking for. The analog controls are aesthetically pleasing, but make selecting an exact temperature impossible (and knowing when the unit is at temperature impossible too). It did, however, make a shockingly good fillet of crispy-skinned salmon.

Sources indicate that rather than a typical basket system, the Crispi consists of a glass container and a PowerPod that sits on top. The idea is that you can store your food directly in the glass containers, and Crispi sets include as many as three basket sizes (with more available). While most food did get crisp in the Crispi (you’d hope so with a name like that!), it took longer to do so than in a standard basket air fryer, and we found that food cooked somewhat unevenly. We tested this unit twice, the second time head-to-head with other glass air fryers, and our biggest gripe remains that there’s no precise temperature control—instead, you must choose between four preset modes (Max Crisp, Bake, Air Fry, and Recrisp). We thought that lack of precision made this model less versatile, and remembering which mode to use for which temperature number recommended on the bag of frozen fries or other foods wasn’t very user-friendly.

Industry observers note that the Typhur Sync has lots of bells and whistles, like a wireless probe thermometer (with a built-in charging port), app compatibility, a PFAS-free basket, and nine total programs (including the three found only in the app). In testing, though, it failed to produce as impressive results as the winning Cosori. The fries browned, but many remained soggy, the salmon skin failed to crisp, and the Brussels sprouts didn’t quite get as golden as we’d have liked. While some of this might be solved by tinkering with time and temperature, at $160, we just didn’t feel this air fryer was worth the splurge.

Industry observers note that in its defense, Magnifique’s Glass Air Fryer has some thoughtful features: two sizes of glass baskets (4.5-qt. and 2.5-qt.), each with lids, and a silicone base that’s easy to remove for cleaning and oven or microwave cooking (something Cuisinart and Ninja can’t match). It’s also the only glass air fryer we tested in this round that could possibly hold a small pizza with an 8.5" diameter crisper plate. However, there are more than a few aspects that weren’t as user-friendly. The stainless-steel crisper plate (no nonstick coating whatsoever) was the most difficult to clean by far, not only because of that lack of coating but because of the perforation pattern as well. The instructions specifically say don’t use scouring pads, but a gentle scrub with a plastic pad was the only way we could remove all the residue. There’s no reminder to flip or shake your food halfway through, a pretty standard-matter beep on many other units, and when you do take the lid off, you have to actually hit Start again to keep going, something other fryers do automatically. Results, especially with frozen foods like fries, were uneven, and fine-tuning is near impossible as its interface only allows for four preset cooking modes with no customization. If you’re following a recipe, you’ll have to remember which mode gets to which general temperature range and hope for the best.

What is an air fryer? Is it just a convection oven?

An air fryer is a countertop oven that uses hot air, circulated by a fan, to give foods crisper textures than you can achieve in a regular oven or toaster oven. What makes an air fryer a “fryer” is a built-in convection fan that blows the hot air around the food to crisp it up. It’s the combination of heat and moving air that produces the kind of crispy exterior you’d otherwise get from deep-frying or pan-frying. But unlike a deep fryer, an air fryer requires far less oil to achieve the desired effect—and it doesn’t leave your house smelling like a grease trap for days or weeks. So, technically speaking, yes, air fryers are just small convection ovens, but the most classic form of air fryer isn’t usually oven-shaped, rather more like egg or block with a slide-out basket on the front.

Whether you’re a purist and only consider products that contain baskets to be true air fryers, or you find the term air fryer to be stupid marketing jargon for a convection oven is up to you to decide. For the purposes of this review, we’ve included both toaster ovens that contain convection or “air fryer” settings and basket or bowl air fryers.

What accessories should I buy for my air fryer?

Sources indicate that there are a few extras you can buy to optimize your frying experience—things like an olive oil sprayer (so you can crisp without spilling oil on the heating element), parchment paper liners, and an instant read thermometer. For more of our favorite air fryer accessories, head right this way.

Sources indicate that alaina Chou: I’ve been testing air fryers and other small appliances for Bon Appétit and Epicurious since 2023. In that time, I’ve cooked countless batches of salmon, brussels sprouts, and frozen fries in pursuit of an air fryer that delivers on the lofty promise of deep-fryer-level crispiness without the need for a vat of hot oil. And I’ve blown out the power in the Test Kitchen numerous times in the process (sorry, Test Kitchen editors).
